meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He who learns but does not think, is lost'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Confucius. It's Analects 2.15; the famous English phrasing is Arthur Waley's 1938 translation of the Classical Chinese original.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 551–479 BCE · Chinese philosopher and teacher; recorded in the Analects
answer.sourceLine: It is a genuine saying of Confucius, preserved as verse 15 of Book 2 (Wei Zheng) of the ‘Analects’ — 學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆. This exact English wording is Arthur Waley’s 1938 translation; other scholars render the same line quite differently.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆

source.excerpt: He who learns but does not think, is lost. He who thinks but does not learn is in great danger.
trail: The Classical Chinese original, 學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆, is verse 15 of Book 2 of the Analects, confirmed against the primary text at the Chinese Text Project ↗.
The exact popular wording — “He who learns but does not think, is lost” — is Arthur Waley’s 1938 translation ↗, one of several English renderings of the same line.
Waley’s published translation of the passage reads exactly this way in the text of his Analects, Book 2, passage 15 ↗.
Unlike countless fabricated “Confucius says” lines online, this one is authentic — the caveat is only that the memorable phrasing belongs to the translator, not to Confucius’ own words.
source.cutTag: ↑ the second half is usually dropped when the line is quoted
source.excerptNote: The couplet is a matched pair: Confucius warns that learning and thinking each fail without the other. The popular quote keeps only the first clause. Because the original is Classical Chinese, the English varies widely by translator — James Legge (1861) gives “Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous,” while James Ware (1950) has “Learning without thought ends in a blur.”

sourceLink.text: The Analects 2.15 at the Chinese Text Project

source.rightsNote: The underlying saying is ancient and in the public domain, as are the pre-1929 English translations by James Legge (1861) and W. E. Soothill (1910). The specific wording quoted here, however, is Arthur Waley’s 1938 translation, which remains under copyright (Waley died in 1966). Quote the Legge or Soothill wording if you need a public-domain English version.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: About Confucius
author.bio: Confucius (Kǒng Fūzǐ, 551–479 BCE) was a teacher and thinker of China’s Spring and Autumn period whose ideas on ethics, learning and government became the foundation of Confucianism. He wrote no book himself; his sayings survive as the Analects (論語), a collection compiled by his disciples and their successors in the generations after his death. Verse 2.15 is one of its most quoted lines on the balance between study and reflection.

misattribution.heading: A note on wording, not authorship
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Confucius is correct — this is a real line from the Analects, not one of the many invented “Confucius says” quotes. The only thing worth flagging is a translation subtlety.

items.why: Confucius spoke and was recorded in Classical Chinese (學而不思則罔). The crisp English “He who learns but does not think, is lost” is Arthur Waley’s 1938 phrasing ↗, not a word-for-word transcription — other translators render the identical line as “labour lost” (Legge) or “ends in a blur” (Ware).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: genuinely Confucius, from Analects 2.15 ↗ — just remember the famous English wording is the translator’s, Arthur Waley’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Verse 2.15 is one of the Analects’ tightest formulations of Confucius’ theory of education: study and reflection are useless apart and powerful together. It reads as a balanced couplet — learning without thought leaves you ‘lost’ or bewildered; thought without learning leaves you in ‘danger.’

Because the line survives only in Classical Chinese, every English version is an act of interpretation. That is why the same nine characters have entered English as “labour lost,” “a blur,” “a waste,” and Waley’s memorable “is lost” — all faithful to the original, none definitive.
context.pull: Learning without thought leaves you lost; thought without learning leaves you in danger.
